title: Level 2 Final Assessment
quiz.0.question: What are the best-known grapes of Alto Adige (South Tyrol) in Trentino-Alto Adige?
quiz.0.options.1: Crisp whites based on Germanic-Austrian aromatic grapes (such as Gewürztraminer and Riesling)
quiz.0.explanation: Alto Adige (Südtirol) was historically part of Austria and German is an official language; it is known for Germanic-Austrian aromatic grapes, especially Gewürztraminer (Traminer Aromatico), Riesling and Pinot Bianco, in crisp, mineral styles reflecting the Alpine mountain climate.
quiz.1.question: Which Italian village does the name Gewürztraminer come from?
quiz.1.explanation: Gewürztraminer's name comes from the village of Tramin (German) / Termeno (Italian) in Alto Adige, and "Gewürz" means spice in German. Traminer is generally believed to be named after this village, and its aromatic mutation Gewürztraminer later flourished in Alsace and elsewhere.
quiz.2.question: What is Friuli Venezia Giulia's Collio DOC known for?
quiz.2.options.1: Some of Italy's finest whites, especially Friulano and skin-contact whites
quiz.2.explanation: Collio DOC (bordering Slovenia's Brda hills) is one of Italy's top white wine areas, famous for Friulano (formerly Tocai Friulano), Ribolla Gialla and skin-contact whites (orange wine); producers such as Josko Gravner pioneered the modern orange-wine movement here.
quiz.3.question: Why was Tocai Friulano forced to change its name to Friulano?
quiz.3.options.0: DNA research found it identical to Sauvignon Blanc
quiz.3.options.1: The EU ruled the name could be confused with Hungary's Tokaj, requiring a change from 2007
quiz.3.options.2: The Italian government pushed to standardise grape names
quiz.3.options.3: Producers voluntarily renamed it to shed associations with sweet wine
quiz.3.explanation: Because the EU ruled that the name could be confused with Hungary's Tokaj (although they are completely different wines), Tocai Friulano had to be renamed Friulano from 2007 — a famous episode of naming politics in Italian wine history.
quiz.4.question: What type of wine is Emilia-Romagna's Lambrusco?
quiz.4.options.0: A dry, concentrated red over 15% alcohol
quiz.4.options.1: A lightly sparkling red, from dry to sweet, fresh and easy
quiz.4.options.2: A traditional-method sparkling white, like Champagne
quiz.4.options.3: A fortified red for after dinner
quiz.4.explanation: Lambrusco is Emilia-Romagna's lightly sparkling red, ranging from dry to sweet, fresh and fruity — the traditional local partner for Prosciutto di Parma and Parmigiano.
quiz.5.question: Emilia-Romagna is called Italy's "food basket". Which of these foods does NOT come from this region?
quiz.5.options.3: Aceto Balsamico di Modena (Modena balsamic vinegar)
quiz.5.explanation: Mozzarella di Bufala Campana PDO comes from Campania, not Emilia-Romagna. Parma ham, Parmigiano and (Modena) balsamic vinegar are the region's signature PDO foods.
quiz.6.question: What is the biggest agricultural challenge facing Liguria's Cinque Terre DOC?
quiz.6.options.0: Overly fertile soils, so vines overgrow and quality is low
quiz.6.options.1: Very low rainfall, with almost no irrigation possible
quiz.6.options.2: Cliff terraces with slopes over 60%, requiring hand harvesting at very high cost
quiz.6.options.3: Frequent pests and diseases, making organic farming difficult
quiz.6.explanation: Cinque Terre's vines grow on almost vertical cliff terraces on the Mediterranean coast, with slopes over 60% that make mechanisation impossible; they rely on hand harvesting and monorails, making them some of the most expensive vineyards in the world to farm.
quiz.7.question: What is the most famous sensory trait of Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi DOC (Marche)?
quiz.7.options.0: High tannin, low acid, with rich oak
quiz.7.options.1: Crisp and high in acid, with a bitter-almond finish and strong minerality
quiz.7.options.2: Sweet, with lychee and rose aromas
quiz.7.explanation: Verdicchio is known for its fresh, high acidity and distinctive bitter-almond finish; Marche's most important white grape, it is especially good with Adriatic seafood and one of Italy's most successfully exported regional white grapes.
quiz.8.question: What is the most outstanding feature of Sagrantino di Montefalco DOCG (Umbria)?
quiz.8.options.0: Italy's lowest-tannin grape, easy and early-drinking
quiz.8.options.1: One of Italy's highest-tannin grapes, with a minimum of 37 months' ageing
quiz.8.options.2: Italy's only DOCG allowed to add foreign grapes
quiz.8.options.3: Passito (sweet, from dried grapes) is its only legal style
quiz.8.explanation: Sagrantino is considered the grape with the highest polyphenol and tannin content in Italy (and perhaps the world); Sagrantino di Montefalco DOCG requires at least 37 months of ageing (including 12 in oak), and it is very closed when young, needing 10-20 years to open fully.
quiz.9.question: What has Frascati DOC (Lazio) traditionally meant to Romans?
quiz.9.options.0: Rome's top collector's wine, drunk only on special occasions
quiz.9.options.1: An everyday house white, the Romans' "table white" for centuries
quiz.9.options.2: Italy's most important DOCG white, rivalling Barolo
quiz.9.options.3: A holy wine traditionally used only in religious rites
quiz.9.explanation: Frascati lies in the Castelli Romani hills of Lazio, about 20 km south of Rome; based on Malvasia and Trebbiano, crisp and easy, it has been the Romans' most approachable everyday white for centuries, a symbol of the wine culture shared by the city and its countryside.
quiz.10.question: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG are easily confused. What is correct?
quiz.10.options.0: They are exactly the same grape, only the place names differ
quiz.10.options.1: The first uses the Montepulciano grape (Abruzzo); the second uses Sangiovese (from the town of Montepulciano in Tuscany)
quiz.10.options.2: The first is the ancient parent of the second
quiz.10.options.3: Both are local variants of Sangiovese with different names
quiz.10.explanation: A common confusion! Montepulciano d'Abruzzo uses the Montepulciano grape; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG, although from the town of Montepulciano in Tuscany, uses Sangiovese (Prugnolo Gentile) — similar names, completely different grapes.
quiz.11.question: Which grape does Campania's Taurasi DOCG use, and what is it called?
quiz.11.explanation: Taurasi DOCG is made from Aglianico, aged at least 3 years (Riserva 4); with high acidity, high tannin and long ageing potential it is called "the Barolo of the south", performing best on the volcanic soils of Irpinia in Campania.
quiz.12.question: Fiano di Avellino DOCG and Greco di Tufo DOCG both come from which province of which region?
quiz.12.explanation: Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo both come from the province of Avellino in Campania (the volcanic hills of Irpinia); they are southern Italy's most important top white DOCGs, known for minerality, complexity and ageing potential.
quiz.13.question: Primitivo (Puglia) is identical by DNA to which American grape, and where is their shared homeland?
quiz.13.explanation: DNA testing in 2001 confirmed that Primitivo is identical to California's Zinfandel; both come from the ancient Croatian grape Tribidrag (or Crljenak Kaštelanski). The name Primitivo comes from the Italian for "first to ripen".
quiz.14.question: What is the style of Puglia's Primitivo di Manduria DOC?
quiz.14.options.0: Italy's lightest red, best served chilled
quiz.14.options.2: A rich red from a warm climate, high in alcohol (14-17%), with black fruit and chocolate
quiz.14.explanation: Primitivo di Manduria reaches very high ripeness in Puglia's sunny Mediterranean climate, making rich reds of 14-17% alcohol full of black fruit, chocolate and spice — southern Italy's most representative rich, high-alcohol red.
quiz.15.question: What does "Vulture" in Basilicata's Aglianico del Vulture DOC refer to?
quiz.15.options.0: The family crest of the estate's founder
quiz.15.options.1: A local bird of prey used as a symbol
quiz.15.options.2: Monte Vulture, an extinct volcano whose volcanic soils are key to quality
quiz.15.explanation: Vulture refers to Monte Vulture, an extinct volcano; Aglianico is grown at 300-700 m on volcanic soils (basalt, tuff), whose minerals give the wine a distinctive ferrous minerality and fresh acidity.
quiz.16.question: Which legend is Calabria's Cirò DOC (made from Gaglioppo) linked to?
quiz.16.options.0: The court wine of Roman emperors
quiz.16.options.1: The victory wine offered to ancient Greek Olympic athletes
quiz.16.options.3: An essential cargo on Venetian trade routes
quiz.16.explanation: Cirò (anciently Cremissa) is said to have been the wine offered to Olympic champions in ancient Greek times, and is called "Italy's oldest wine"; it reflects the history of Magna Graecia in southern Italy and is Calabria's best-known DOC.
quiz.17.question: Sardinia's Cannonau DOC uses the Cannonau grape, which is identical by DNA to which international grape?
quiz.17.explanation: Cannonau is Grenache / Garnacha; some researchers argue that Sardinia may be its homeland, but most still believe it originated in Spain (Garnacha) and spread to southern France (Grenache) and Sardinia.
quiz.18.question: What are the flavours of Vermentino di Sardegna DOC?
quiz.18.options.0: A rich, heavy red for beef stew
quiz.18.options.1: A crisp white with Mediterranean notes of honey, fennel and almond
quiz.18.options.2: A sweet fortified white, like sherry
quiz.18.options.3: A pink sparkling wine, Italy's most famous rosé
quiz.18.explanation: Vermentino di Sardegna is Sardinia's signature white, with honey, fennel, aloe and almond and a slightly bitter finish typical of the grape; a perfect match for Mediterranean seafood and the white Sardinians are proudest of.
quiz.19.question: What is the main way traditionalists (tradizionalisti) make Barolo?
quiz.19.options.0: Short maceration (3-5 days), aged in small French barriques
quiz.19.options.1: Long maceration (30-60 days), aged in large Slavonian oak casks (botti grandi)
quiz.19.options.2: Destemmed cold maceration with precise temperature control
quiz.19.options.3: Adding Barbera for colour and fruit
quiz.19.explanation: Traditionalists (Giacomo Conterno, Bartolo Mascarello and others) insist on long macerations of 30-60 days to extract maximum tannin and age the wine for a long time in large Slavonian oak casks (botti, often holding several thousand litres), giving powerful, complex wines with great ageing potential.
quiz.20.question: What is the main way modernists (modernisti) make Barolo?
quiz.20.options.0: Quick extraction in rotary fermenters and ageing in small French barriques, for fruity wines that open early
quiz.20.options.3: Adding spirit to raise the alcohol
quiz.20.explanation: Modernists (Elio Altare, Roberto Voerzio and others) use rotary fermenters for quick extraction (7-15 days of maceration) and small French barriques (225 litres) for sweet vanilla and mocha notes; the wines open earlier and suit younger drinking.
quiz.21.question: What was Angelo Gaja's most revolutionary contribution to Italian wine?
quiz.21.options.1: Introducing French barriques and the single-vineyard concept in Barbaresco, opening the international stage to Italian wine
quiz.21.options.3: Creating Italy's first wine scoring system
quiz.21.explanation: In the 1970s-80s Angelo Gaja introduced French barriques and the single-vineyard concept (Sorì Tildìn, Sorì San Lorenzo, Costa Russi) in Barbaresco and actively took Italian wine to the high-end international market; he is seen as a key figure in changing the fortunes of Italian wine.
quiz.22.question: Why could Sassicaia at first only be labelled Vino da Tavola?
quiz.22.options.0: The owner deliberately chose the lowest level out of modesty
quiz.22.options.1: It used non-permitted grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon and met no DOC rules
quiz.22.options.2: The Bolgheri appellation did not yet exist in 1968
quiz.22.explanation: Sassicaia is made from Bordeaux grapes (Cabernet Sauvignon + Cabernet Franc); because it met no Italian DOC/DOCG rules, it could only be labelled Vino da Tavola when first released commercially in 1968, until it gained its own Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC in 1994.
quiz.23.question: What does the ripasso technique do in Valpolicella (Veneto)?
quiz.23.options.0: Filters out colour from the juice to make rosé
quiz.23.options.1: Pours Valpolicella base wine back over the moist pomace left from Amarone for a second fermentation that adds complexity
quiz.23.options.2: Uses rotary fermenters to extract tannin quickly
quiz.23.options.3: Pumps juice under high pressure from old barrels into new ones
quiz.23.explanation: Ripasso ("passed over again"): Valpolicella Classico base wine is poured over the moist pomace left after making Amarone and refermented for 10-15 days, absorbing residual sugar, tannin and flavour to make a wine between Valpolicella and Amarone, called "the poor man's Amarone".
quiz.24.question: What is the main difference between Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG and Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG?
quiz.24.options.1: Recioto stops fermentation to keep residual sugar (sweet), while Amarone ferments fully to dryness (dry)
quiz.24.options.2: Recioto is aged in stainless steel, Amarone in wood
quiz.24.options.3: Recioto is made only in certain vintages
quiz.24.explanation: Both use dried grapes (appassimento), but Recioto is stopped before fermentation finishes (keeping residual sugar) and is sweet, while Amarone ferments fully to dryness ("amaro" = bitter). Amarone is said to have been discovered by accident when a Recioto fermented too far.
quiz.25.question: How important are Italian wine co-operatives (cantine cooperative)?
quiz.25.options.0: They only make low-quality everyday wine and no DOCG wines
quiz.25.options.1: They account for about 55-60% of Italy's total wine production and are the main outlet for small rural growers
quiz.25.options.2: They exist only in Sicily and Sardinia
quiz.25.options.3: They have shrunk sharply, now under 10% of production
quiz.25.explanation: Italian co-operatives produce about 55-60% of the country's wine and are a key structure for the survival of small rural growers. Some high-quality co-operatives even make fine DOCG wines — Trentino's co-operatives, for example, dominate local DOC production — so they cannot all be assumed to be low quality.
quiz.26.question: By value, what are the top three destination markets for Italian wine exports?
quiz.26.options.1: The US, Germany, the UK (or Switzerland)
quiz.26.explanation: The US, Germany and the UK (rankings sometimes shift slightly) are Italian wine's largest export markets by value. The US market has strong demand for premium DOCGs and Super Tuscans, while Germany is a major market for everyday whites such as Pinot Grigio.
quiz.27.question: What is the link between Sardinia's Cannonau and "Blue Zone" longevity research?
quiz.27.options.0: There is no scientific basis; it is tourism marketing
quiz.27.options.1: Sardinia is one of the world's five Blue Zones, and researchers suggest Cannonau's rich polyphenols may benefit cardiovascular health
quiz.27.options.2: The WHO recognises Cannonau as the only wine good for the heart
quiz.27.options.3: Science has fully confirmed that a daily glass of Cannonau adds 10 years of life
quiz.27.explanation: The Barbagia mountains of Sardinia are one of the world's five Blue Zones, with a very high proportion of centenarians. Researchers note that the locals' moderate daily drinking of Cannonau (rich in polyphenols and anthocyanins) may have a protective cardiovascular effect, but this remains an area of research, not a firm conclusion.
quiz.28.question: Which description of the history of southern Italian wine is most accurate?
quiz.28.options.0: Before Italian unification the south produced very little wine and hardly exported any
quiz.28.options.1: The south long supplied high-alcohol, rich reds to the north (and even southern France) as blending wines for colour
quiz.28.options.2: Because of severe pests and diseases, the south only began growing vines in the 20th century
quiz.28.options.3: Southern wines have always been known for light whites, more popular in Europe than northern wines
quiz.28.explanation: Thanks to strong sun, the south (especially Puglia and Sicily) traditionally produced large volumes of high-alcohol, concentrated reds that long served as blending wines to bolster northern DOC/DOCG wines, and were even exported to southern France to add colour and alcohol to weak vintages. This era of "anonymous colouring" only changed gradually after the 1980s-90s as the south grew in self-confidence.
quiz.29.question: Which region is NOT part of the Level 2 northern course (Trentino-Alto Adige, Friuli, Liguria, Emilia-Romagna)?
quiz.29.explanation: Campania is a southern region, part of the Level 2 southern course, known for Taurasi DOCG (Aglianico) and its Fiano / Greco whites; Trentino-Alto Adige, Friuli Venezia Giulia, Liguria and Emilia-Romagna are the four regions of the Level 2 northern course.
quiz.30.question: Nero d'Avola and Nerello Mascalese are both signature Sicilian grapes. What is the main style difference?
quiz.30.options.0: Nerello is richer than Nero d'Avola, deeper in colour and higher in tannin
quiz.30.options.1: Nero d'Avola is rich and full (Syrah-like), Nerello light, elegant, high in acid and mineral (Pinot Noir-like)
quiz.30.options.2: The two wines are almost indistinguishable
quiz.30.options.3: Nerello can only make rosé, Nero d'Avola only red
quiz.30.explanation: In the warm conditions of Sicily's lowlands, Nero d'Avola makes rich, full reds similar to Syrah; Nerello Mascalese, in the cool, high conditions of Etna (600-1,000 m), makes light, high-acid, strongly mineral and elegant reds, often likened to Italy's Pinot Noir.
quiz.31.question: Which statement about Barolo's MGA (Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive) system is correct?
quiz.31.options.0: It is an organic certification standard; MGA means pesticide-free land
quiz.31.options.1: It is a vineyard geographical designation system set up in 2010, an Italian take on the Premier Cru concept
quiz.31.options.2: It applies only to Barbaresco DOCG, not Barolo
quiz.31.options.3: It is an acronym for Italian export rules limiting Barolo export quotas
quiz.31.explanation: MGAs (Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive) are an official vineyard designation system (Barbaresco in 2007, Barolo in 2010) that names and standardises the important vineyards of each village, similar to Burgundy's Premier Cru concept; on a label they indicate wine from a specific site, such as Barolo MGA Cannubi or Brunate.
quiz.32.question: Where is Italian en primeur (futures) most active?
quiz.32.options.0: Veneto, because Amarone needs long ageing
quiz.32.options.2: Piemonte, because Barolo futures trading began earliest
quiz.32.options.3: Sicily, because Etna wines are the most fashionable
quiz.32.explanation: Top Tuscan wines (Super Tuscans such as Sassicaia, Ornellaia and Masseto, plus Brunello di Montalcino) are the most active in Italian futures trading; several Super Tuscans are even released en primeur through Bordeaux's La Place, attracting collectors and investors worldwide.
quiz.33.question: For which style has Umbria's Orvieto DOC (mainly Grechetto and Trebbiano) traditionally been most famous?
quiz.33.options.0: Dry, heavy reds aged over 10 years
quiz.33.options.1: Crisp dry or off-dry whites, among central Italy's most famous whites
quiz.33.options.3: Pink sparkling wine, central Italy's most important rosé
quiz.33.explanation: Orvieto DOC is one of the most important whites of Umbria and central Italy, based on Grechetto and Trebbiano; traditionally made dry (secco) and off-dry (abboccato), crisp and easy, it was the favourite table wine of the medieval papal court (Orvieto was once a temporary papal seat).

slides.1.title: 📚 Scope and Instructions
slides.1.content:
This assessment covers the advanced knowledge of all Level 2 lessons, with 34 questions.

🏔️ Four northern regions: Trentino-Alto Adige, Friuli, Liguria, Emilia-Romagna
🌿 Five central regions: Marche, Umbria, Lazio, Abruzzo, Molise
☀️ Five southern regions: Campania, Puglia, Basilicata, Calabria, Sardinia
🍇 Grapes in depth: Aglianico, Primitivo / Zinfandel, Cannonau / Grenache
📈 Markets and collecting: futures, co-operatives, export markets

Suggested time: 45 minutes | Pass mark: 70 (at least 24 correct answers)
slides.2.title: 🎯 Level 2 Key Review
slides.2.points.0: 🏔️ Alto Adige: Germanic-Austrian aromatic grapes (Gewürztraminer from the village of Tramin / Termeno)
slides.2.points.1: 🍸 Friuli: Tocai Friulano → renamed Friulano (an EU naming dispute with Hungary's Tokaj)
slides.2.points.2: 🍊 Friuli's Collio DOC: a hub of fine whites + a pioneer of modern orange wine (Josko Gravner)
slides.2.points.3: ⛵ Liguria: Cinque Terre cliff terraces, slopes of 60%+, very costly hand harvesting
slides.2.points.4: 🍖 Emilia-Romagna: lightly sparkling Lambrusco + Italy's food basket
slides.2.points.5: 🌊 Marche: Verdicchio's bitter-almond finish + a golden match with Adriatic seafood
slides.2.points.6: 🏛️ Umbria: Sagrantino (Italy's king of tannin, 37 months' minimum ageing)
slides.2.points.7: 🏛️ Lazio: Frascati, Rome's everyday white for centuries (Malvasia + Trebbiano)
slides.2.points.8: ⚠️ Name trap: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo (grape) ≠ Vino Nobile di Montepulciano (a Tuscan place, made from Sangiovese)
slides.2.points.9: 🔥 Campania: Taurasi DOCG (Aglianico) = the Barolo of the south
slides.2.points.10: 🤍 Campania's two whites: Fiano di Avellino + Greco di Tufo (volcanic hills of the province of Avellino)
slides.2.points.11: 🌞 Puglia: Primitivo = Zinfandel (from Croatia's Tribidrag, confirmed by DNA in 2001)
slides.2.points.12: 🌋 Basilicata: Aglianico del Vulture (volcanic soils of Monte Vulture)
slides.2.points.13: ⚔️ Calabria: Cirò DOC Gaglioppo (the legend of the ancient Greek Olympic wine)
slides.2.points.14: 🏖️ Sardinia: Cannonau = Grenache (some researchers argue Sardinia is its homeland)
slides.2.points.15: 🌿 Sardinia: Vermentino, a crisp Mediterranean white + Blue Zone longevity research
slides.2.points.16: ⚖️ The Barolo wars: traditionalists (long maceration + large botti) vs modernists (short maceration + barriques)
slides.2.points.17: 🦁 The Gaja revolution: Barbaresco single vineyards + French barriques → Italian wine goes international
slides.2.points.18: 📜 Sassicaia: the forerunner of the Super Tuscans, in 1994 the first DOC covering a single estate
slides.2.points.19: 🍷 Ripasso = Valpolicella refermented over Amarone pomace
slides.2.points.20: 🍯 Recioto (sweet) vs Amarone (fully dry) — the same technique, different fermentation end points
slides.2.points.21: 🏭 Co-operatives make about 55-60% of Italy's total production
slides.2.points.22: 📊 Top three export markets: the US, Germany, the UK
slides.2.points.23: 📈 Most active futures: top Tuscan wines (Sassicaia, Ornellaia, Brunello)
